newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ economist turned MP warns of Japan recession.
newsitem.headline: BOJ economist turned MP warns of Japan recession.

text.p: Japan's economy is likely to slip into recession if the government goes ahead with its planned budget for the year starting in April, says a former economist at the Bank of Japan (BOJ) who is now a member of parliament.

"The risk is high that the economy will slow down in the first half (of the next fiscal year) and fall into a recession in the latter half," said Yoshio Suzuki, a Lower House member with the key opposition New Frontier Party (Shinshinto).
Argument over the budget for the fiscal year starting on April 1 centres on a rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent and the end of special cuts in income tax.
Suzuki, speaking in an interview earlier this week, said the two moves would dampen consumer spending and push the economy into a crisis.

"It will lead to all sorts of problems -- unemployment, bankruptcies and a fall in stock prices," said Suzuki, a former executive with the central bank who also later worked for Nomura Research Institute.

Tokyo stock prices have fallen sharply since the end of last year on worries over the outlook for the economy. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate hit a record high of 3.4 percent last year amid the slow recovery in the economy.
Suzuki rebutted the government's view that the economy would overcome the negative effects of the fiscal tightening and accomplish its goal of 1.9 percent growth for the year.

"The Japanese economy will face a time of crisis. In order to avert that, we must stimulate the economy from the supply side," Suzuki said. Supply side economics is a theory that tax cuts and similar measures boost investment in production and increase the supply of goods in an economy.
But the government has abandoned its habit of supporting the economy through stimulus packages centred on public works, stressing the need to improve its debt-ridden fiscal finances.

The 77.39 trillion yen ($624 billion) budget, up 3.0 percent from the budget for the current year, keeps growth in public works spending to a meagre 1.3 percent and cuts government bond issues by four trillion yen ($32.2 billion).
Suzuki said priority should instead be given to supporting the economy. "There's a clear danger for the economy. How can we sit here idle and do nothing about it," he said.
He personally believed a tax cut of 18 trillion yen ($145 billion) was vital to lift the economy, and it should be financed by deficit-financing bonds.

But he said Shinshinto would for the time being try to form an alliance with other opposition parties and call for tax cuts of nearly three trillion yen ($24.1 billion), including continuation of the special income tax cut.
The tax cuts would be financed by slashing unnecessary spending in the budget, he said.

The government has so far refused to accept any changes in the budget, playing down the effects of the fiscal tightening as temporary and sticking to the view that the economy will overcome it and remain on a recovery track.
Shinshinto has around 150 seats out of the total 500 in the Lower House, making it the largest opposition party in the key legislative chamber. ($1=124 yen)
